quiz.title: Unit 6 DBQ: New ideas and old hierarchies
quiz.headline: New ideas and old hierarchies
quiz.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which new ideas about government, labor, and economic life challenged existing social and political hierarchies in the period 1750–1900.
quiz.instructions: Use at least four documents to support an argument. For at least two documents, explain how the author's point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience is relevant to your argument. Use at least one piece of specific historical evidence beyond the documents. Include contextualization and develop a complex argument. This is untimed self-assessment practice in AP format.
quiz.note: Original Page One practice. Rubric categories follow the structure of the College Board's AP history rubrics; scoring here is your own self-assessment, not an official score.

rubric.label: Thesis
rubric.guidance: Responds to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.

rubric.label: Contextualization
rubric.guidance: Describes a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.

rubric.label: Evidence from the documents
rubric.guidance: 1 point: accurately describes the content of at least three documents to address the prompt. 2 points: uses the content of at least four documents to support an argument in response to the prompt.

rubric.label: Evidence beyond the documents
rubric.guidance: Uses at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence, not found in the documents, that is relevant to an argument about the prompt.

rubric.label: Sourcing
rubric.guidance: For at least two documents, explains how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience is relevant to an argument.

rubric.label: Complexity
rubric.guidance: Demonstrates a complex understanding of the topic, using evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument.

scaffold.label: Read
scaffold.text: Note each document's author, date, and purpose before its content.

scaffold.label: Group
scaffold.text: Sort documents by the claim they support, not by their order.

scaffold.label: Argue
scaffold.text: Use documents as evidence and explain how each supports your claim.

scaffold.label: Source
scaffold.text: Explain why point of view, purpose, situation, or audience matters for two documents.

scaffold.label: Qualify
scaffold.text: Show where the pattern varied by region or social group.

documents.label: A pamphlet for American independence
documents.attribution: Thomas Paine, English-born writer living in Philadelphia, Common Sense, pamphlet published in January 1776
documents.content:
The cause of America is in a great measure the cause of all mankind. . . .

Society in every state is a blessing, but government even in its best state is but a necessary evil; in its worst state an intolerable one . . . .

Small islands not capable of protecting themselves, are the proper objects for kingdoms to take under their care; but there is something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island. . . .

O ye that love mankind! Ye that dare oppose, not only the tyranny, but the tyrant, stand forth! Every spot of the old world is overrun with oppression. Freedom hath been hunted round the globe.
documents.citation: Thomas Paine, Common Sense (1776), introduction and parts 1 and 3. Project Gutenberg eBook #147.
documents.note: “The continent” is the thirteen British colonies in North America; “the island” is Great Britain.
documents.sourceNote: Excerpt text is reused unchanged from Page One's excerpt library, where it is checked against the edition named in the citation.

documents.label: Division of labor in a pin factory
documents.attribution: Adam Smith, Scottish philosopher and economist, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, 1776
documents.content: One man draws out the wire; another straights it; a third cuts it; a fourth points it; a fifth grinds it at the top for receiving the head; to make the head requires two or three distinct operations; to put it on is a peculiar business; to whiten the pins is another; it is even a trade by itself to put them into the paper; and the important business of making a pin is, in this manner, divided into about eighteen distinct operations, which, in some manufactories, are all performed by distinct hands, though in others the same man will sometimes perform two or three of them. I have seen a small manufactory of this kind, where ten men only were employed, and where some of them consequently performed two or three distinct operations.
documents.citation: Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, ch. 1. Project Gutenberg eBook #3300.
documents.note: A manufactory is a workshop. Smith is describing the division of labor in pin-making.
documents.sourceNote: Excerpt text is reused unchanged from Page One's excerpt library, where it is checked against the edition named in the citation.

metadata.author: Adam Smith
metadata.setting: Great Britain, at the start of the Industrial Revolution

documents.label: A call for women's education
documents.attribution: Mary Wollstonecraft, English writer, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792
documents.content:
It is time to effect a revolution in female manners, time to restore to them their lost dignity, and make them, as a part of the human species, labour by reforming themselves to reform the world. . . .

[Women] would be more respectable members of society, and discharge the important duties of life by the light of their own reason. "Educate women like men," says Rousseau, "and the more they resemble our sex the less power will they have over us." This is the very point I aim at. I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.
documents.citation: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, chs. 3–4. Project Gutenberg eBook #3420.
documents.note: Wollstonecraft is responding to the French Enlightenment writer Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who argued that women should be educated to please men. Bracketed words replace “they.”
documents.sourceNote: Excerpt text is reused unchanged from Page One's excerpt library, where it is checked against the edition named in the citation.

documents.label: Class struggle and the factory worker
documents.attribution: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, German political philosophers, Manifesto of the Communist Party, 1848
documents.content:
The history of all hitherto existing societies is the history of class struggles. . . .

The need of a constantly expanding market for its products chases the bourgeoisie over the whole surface of the globe. It must nestle everywhere, settle everywhere, establish connexions everywhere. . . .

Owing to the extensive use of machinery and to division of labour, the work of the proletarians has lost all individual character, and consequently, all charm for the workman. He becomes an appendage of the machine . . . .

Let the ruling classes tremble at a Communistic revolution. The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win.
documents.citation: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, Manifesto of the Communist Party, English edition of 1888, trans. Samuel Moore, sections I and IV. Project Gutenberg eBook #61.
documents.note: The bourgeoisie are the owners of factories and capital; the proletarians are industrial wage workers.
documents.sourceNote: Excerpt text is reused unchanged from Page One's excerpt library, where it is checked against the edition named in the citation.

documents.label: The value of self-help
documents.attribution: Samuel Smiles, Scottish writer and reformer, Self-Help, first published in 1859
documents.content: "HEAVEN helps those who help themselves" is a well-tried maxim, embodying in a small compass the results of vast human experience. The spirit of self-help is the root of all genuine growth in the individual; and, exhibited in the lives of many, it constitutes the true source of national vigour and strength. Help from without is often enfeebling in its effects, but help from within invariably invigorates. Whatever is done for men or classes, to a certain extent takes away the stimulus and necessity of doing for themselves; and where men are subjected to over-guidance and over-government, the inevitable tendency is to render them comparatively helpless.
documents.citation: Samuel Smiles, Self-Help (London: John Murray, 1897), ch. 1. Project Gutenberg eBook #935.
documents.sourceNote: Excerpt text is reused unchanged from Page One's excerpt library, where it is checked against the edition named in the citation.

metadata.author: Samuel Smiles
metadata.audience: Working-class and middle-class readers seeking self-improvement

documents.label: Capitalism and the world market
documents.attribution: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, German political philosophers, Manifesto of the Communist Party, 1848
documents.content: The bourgeoisie, by the rapid improvement of all instruments of production, by the immensely facilitated means of communication, draws all, even the most barbarian, nations into civilisation. The cheap prices of its commodities are the heavy artillery with which it batters down all Chinese walls, with which it forces the barbarians' intensely obstinate hatred of foreigners to capitulate. It compels all nations, on pain of extinction, to adopt the bourgeois mode of production . . . . In one word, it creates a world after its own image.
documents.citation: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, Manifesto of the Communist Party, English edition of 1888, trans. Samuel Moore, section I. Project Gutenberg eBook #61.
documents.note: The bourgeoisie are the owners of capital. Marx and Engels use words such as “barbarian” sarcastically, echoing how European capitalists described other peoples. “Chinese walls” refers to China's limits on foreign trade.
documents.sourceNote: Excerpt text is reused unchanged from Page One's excerpt library, where it is checked against the edition named in the citation.

documents.label: Liberty and “backward” societies
documents.attribution: John Stuart Mill, British philosopher and official of the East India Company from 1823 to 1858, On Liberty, 1859
documents.content: It is, perhaps, hardly necessary to say that this doctrine is meant to apply only to human beings in the maturity of their faculties. . . . For the same reason, we may leave out of consideration those backward states of society in which the race itself may be considered as in its nonage. . . . Despotism is a legitimate mode of government in dealing with barbarians, provided the end be their improvement, and the means justified by actually effecting that end. Liberty, as a principle, has no application to any state of things anterior to the time when mankind have become capable of being improved by free and equal discussion. Until then, there is nothing for them but implicit obedience to an Akbar or a Charlemagne, if they are so fortunate as to find one.
documents.citation: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, ch. 1, Introductory. Project Gutenberg eBook #34901.
documents.note: “This doctrine” is Mill's principle that people should be free to act as they choose unless they harm others. “Nonage” means childhood or immaturity. Akbar was the Mughal emperor.
documents.sourceNote: Excerpt text is reused unchanged from Page One's excerpt library, where it is checked against the edition named in the citation.

quiz.modelResponse:
In 1750, most societies were organized around hierarchies of birth: monarchs and nobles ruled, women had few legal rights, and European empires governed colonies overseas. The Enlightenment questioned those arrangements by arguing that people had natural rights and that reason, not tradition, should guide government. Soon afterward, the Industrial Revolution created factories, a wage-earning working class, and a new middle class that sought influence.

Between 1750 and 1900, new ideas about government, labor, and economic life challenged hierarchies based on birth and monarchy, but they also created or justified new hierarchies of class, gender, and empire, so the challenge was significant but uneven.

Several documents show direct challenges to traditional authority. Thomas Paine argued that "society in every state is a blessing, but government even in its best state is but a necessary evil" and mocked the idea that a continent should be governed by an island (Document 1). Writing as a pamphleteer in Philadelphia in 1776, Paine wanted to persuade ordinary colonists to support independence, so he used plain, forceful language, and his claim that freedom had been "hunted round the globe" was meant to move readers more than to describe every case accurately. Even so, the American Declaration of Independence soon echoed his challenge to hereditary authority. Mary Wollstonecraft extended the logic of reason to gender, demanding "a revolution in female manners" and women's power "over themselves" (Document 3). Because she was responding to Rousseau and wrote for educated readers, her argument focused on education rather than political rights, and she did not claim that women should rule men. Olympe de Gouges's Declaration of the Rights of Woman (1791) shows that some contemporaries asked for more.

Ideas about labor and the economy also unsettled older hierarchies. Marx and Engels described history as "the history of class struggles" and called on workers to overthrow their rulers (Document 4). Writing for a political organization in 1848, they had reason to emphasize conflict and to treat workers as a unified force, which most British workers were not at the time. Samuel Smiles, in contrast, told readers that growth came from individual effort and that excessive government help made people "helpless" (Document 5). Writing for readers hoping to rise, Smiles challenged the idea that birth fixed a person's place, but he also argued against state help, a position that fit the interests of a growing middle class. Adam Smith's account of pin-making (Document 2) shows how the division of labor increased output, laying groundwork for factory production that would create both new wealth and the workers whom Marx described as an "appendage of the machine."

However, new ideas also reinforced hierarchies. Marx and Engels observed that capitalism "compels all nations" to adopt its mode of production (Document 6), but they also portrayed European industry as forcing other societies into a subordinate position. Mill, an official of the East India Company, argued that liberty applied only to people capable of improvement by free discussion and that despotism was legitimate for "barbarians" (Document 7). Because he worked for the company that governed much of India, his view helped justify colonial rule at a time when Britain was expanding its empire. The Indian Rebellion of 1857 and the partition of Africa after 1884 show how liberal states applied liberty selectively.

In conclusion, new ideas weakened hierarchies based on birth and absolute monarchy, but they also created class divisions and gave new justifications for empire, so they challenged existing hierarchies without ending inequality.

modelNotes.label: Contextualization
modelNotes.text: The first paragraph describes birth-based hierarchies, the Enlightenment, and the start of industrialization.

modelNotes.label: Thesis
modelNotes.text: The thesis makes a qualified claim about the extent of change and previews two lines of reasoning: challenges to old hierarchies and the creation of new ones.

modelNotes.label: Evidence from the documents
modelNotes.text: All seven documents are used to support the argument and are grouped by claim.

modelNotes.label: Evidence beyond the documents
modelNotes.text: The Declaration of Independence, Olympe de Gouges's declaration, the Indian Rebellion of 1857, and the partition of Africa are specific evidence not found in the documents.

modelNotes.label: Sourcing
modelNotes.text: The essay explains Paine's purpose and audience, Wollstonecraft's response to Rousseau, the purpose of Marx and Engels's pamphlet, Smiles's audience, and Mill's employment by the East India Company.

modelNotes.label: Complexity
modelNotes.text: The argument shows how ideas challenged some hierarchies while creating or justifying others, and it uses outside evidence to qualify the documents.

quiz.alternateModel: A different strong essay could argue that economic ideas changed society more than political ideas, grouping Documents 2, 4, 5, and 6 as evidence of a new industrial order and Documents 1 and 3 as demands that took longer to change law.
commonErrors: Summarizing each document in order instead of grouping them by claim.
Treating Marx and Engels as speaking for all workers.
Quoting Mill without noting his employment by the East India Company.
Writing “the author is biased” without explaining how that affects the argument.
